title: Caching
concept: A cache keeps a copy of data closer to the reader than the source of truth, so most reads skip the slow path. The price is staleness: every write now has to reach the cache too, either by invalidating the old entry or by letting it expire, and races between reads, writes, and invalidations can leave the cache holding a value the database no longer has.

points: A cache serves repeat reads from a copy kept close to the readers, so most reads skip the slow path to the database.
A write does not update the cache by itself, so entries must be invalidated or expire, and races between fills and invalidations can leave an old value behind.
Uber built its cache inside the database and used the database's own change log as the signal to invalidate entries.
Meta counts only inconsistencies a client could actually observe, and its checker caught a rare bug in an error-handling path.

figures.label: over 10 trillion cache fills a day if the hit rate reached 99%
99.99% consistent once Flux invalidated the cache

prerequisiteReasons.load-balancing: Load balancing shows requests spread over a pool of servers. A cache is one more server in that path, one that answers in place of the origin.

digest.problem: A cache only stays correct if every change in the database reaches it as an invalidation, and races can break that. In Meta's example, a cache fill reads a value, the value then changes, the invalidation for the new value arrives first, and the delayed fill writes the old value back, leaving the cache wrong until something else evicts it. Such races are rare, but the harm can be real: Meta describes a case from well before its 2022 post, when TAO was less consistent, where two people's messages to the same user were sent to different regions.
digest.constraints: Meta's TAO cache handles more than a quadrillion queries a day, so even rare races add up. Logging every cache change would turn a read-heavy cache workload into a write-heavy one for the logging system. Checking the database directly is expensive and could overload it. Any measurement had to be free of false alarms and precise enough to count past ten nines.

walkthrough.explanation: Polaris, a separate service, receives the same invalidation events the cache does and otherwise behaves like an ordinary client.
After an invalidation, Polaris asks every cache replica for the key and flags any replica still returning an older version.

A flagged sample is requeued and checked again. If it is still wrong at a timescale boundary (the post's examples are one, five and ten minutes), it is reported for that timescale, so normal lag is not counted.
Checks that bypass the cache to read the database are delayed and limited, and a query flag shows whether a replica has processed the invalidation yet.
Results are expressed as how many nines of cache writes are consistent within a given number of minutes.

Separately, a tracing library embedded in a few major cache services and the invalidation pipeline logs only the short window after a write when races happen, plus evictions, giving engineers a timeline when Polaris alarms.

tradeoffs.chosen: Measure only inconsistencies a client could observe, using sampled checks after invalidations, retries over several timescales, and tracing limited to the race window.
tradeoffs.rejected: Logging every cache state change, and checking the database immediately for every suspicious sample.
tradeoffs.why: Full logging would turn a read-heavy cache into a write-heavy load on the logging system, and checking the database for every suspicious sample is compute-heavy and puts the database at risk. The cost of waiting is that real problems are reported at a timescale boundary, not instantly; the post presents the wait as part of keeping the metric free of false alarms.

digest.failures: Polaris caught a real bug: a rare transaction updated metadata and version together, a fill slipped in with old metadata, the next invalidation hit a transient error, and the error handler's drop-cache call only removed entries with a lower version. The stale entry carried the current version, so it stayed. Tracing showed the whole sequence and engineers found the cause in under 30 minutes. The authors list promotions, shard moves, failure recoveries, network partitions and hardware failures as events that can trigger bugs leading to inconsistency.
digest.takeaways: Measure what a client could actually observe, and keep the metric free of false alarms so people trust it. Expect some lag and retry before running expensive checks. The rare bug Polaris caught hid in an error-handling path, and running a consistent cache in production is a different problem from designing one.

posts.title: How Uber Serves Over 40 Million Reads Per Second from Online Storage Using an Integrated Cache

digest.problem: Docstore, Uber's distributed database built on MySQL, stores tens of petabytes and serves tens of millions of requests per second. One service needed far more read throughput than Docstore could cheaply provide, and teams that cached on their own each ran a separate Redis cluster, wrote their own invalidation, and, on a regional failover, either had to run their own cache replication to stay warm or accept slow reads while the new region's cache filled.
digest.constraints: Docstore splits into a stateless query engine and a stateful storage engine. Each data partition has a leader and two followers kept in sync with Raft, and every write is replicated to a second active region. The post says scaling costs are multiplied 6x across those nodes and both regions. Docstore promises strong consistency, which a cache can weaken. Some writes are conditional updates, where the database only learns which rows change when it runs the filter, so the query engine cannot know what to invalidate.

walkthrough.explanation: The cache lives in Docstore's query engine. Reads check Redis first, fetch any missing rows from the storage engine, and fill Redis in the background, so services get caching without writing any cache code.
Caching is switched on per database, table or request. Flows that need strong consistency, such as getting items in an eater's cart, skip it.
Entries expire after 5 minutes by default even if no invalidation arrives.

Flux, Docstore's change data capture service, follows MySQL's binary log, and a new consumer invalidates or updates the affected rows in Redis. That covers conditional updates, and uncommitted transactions cannot pollute the cache. The post says this made the cache consistent within seconds of a database change, not minutes.
Both the read path and Flux write to Redis, so a slow fill could overwrite newer data. A small Redis script compares each row's MySQL timestamp and keeps only the newer one.
After a simple write, callers can invalidate rows themselves, so a service reads back what it just wrote.
A compare mode shadows cached reads against the database and reports mismatches.
Only cache keys are copied to the other region, which fills its own cache from its own database, so a failover does not land on a cold cache.

Redis is sharded by partition key, unlike the database, so one Redis cluster going down spreads its load across all database shards. A circuit breaker skips a Redis node that keeps failing, and an adaptive timeout set near the 99.99th percentile of cache latency cancels the slowest requests and serves them from the database.

tradeoffs.chosen: One cache built into the database's query layer, filled on reads, invalidated from the binary log, protected by row versions, and switched off for flows that need strong consistency.
tradeoffs.rejected: Separate Redis caches run by each team, a shorter expiry time, invalidating in the write path, copying cached values between regions with Redis replication, and sharding Redis the same way as the database.
tradeoffs.why: A shorter expiry would cut the hit rate without meaningfully improving consistency, and write-path invalidation cannot see which rows a conditional update touches. Copying values between regions would add a second replication system that could disagree with the database, while copying keys lets each region fill from its own data. The cost is eventual consistency for cached reads, which is why caching is opt-in.

digest.failures: The first invalidation design had a flaw: the read path and the log consumer both write to Redis, so a slow fill could overwrite a newer row. Comparing the MySQL timestamp on each row fixed it. Following the log alone also did not let a service read its own write, so an explicit invalidation call was added. Fixed timeouts were either too short, wasting work, or too long, hurting tail latency, which led to adaptive ones.
digest.takeaways: Putting the cache inside the database means teams share one cache and one invalidation path instead of building their own. Following the database's change log gave Uber faster invalidation than relying on expiry alone and kept uncommitted data out of the cache. A cache needs explicit ways to keep stale data out and a way to measure how often it fails, and a read-heavy workload can be served from relatively cheap hosts once that is in place.

glossary.definition: A hit is a read served from the cache; a miss has to go to the source of truth.
Writing a value into the cache after a miss, using what the database returned.
A message telling the cache an entry is out of date, so it is deleted or replaced.
Time to live: how long an entry may be served before it expires on its own.
glossary.diagram: <svg viewBox="0 0 560 110" role="img" aria-labelledby="dg-ca-gl-ttl-t" class="dg"><title id="dg-ca-gl-ttl-t">TTL: an entry may be served from the time it is written until its time to live runs out, then it expires on its own.</title><defs><marker id="dg-ca-gl-ttl-a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M1,1 L9,5 L1,9" class="dg-head"/></marker></defs><text x="14" y="20" class="dg-note" text-anchor="start" font-size="11">entry written</text><text x="384" y="20" class="dg-note" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11">TTL runs out</text><rect x="14" y="30" width="370" height="40" class="dg-box dg-accent"/><text x="199" y="54.55" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">May be served</text><rect x="394" y="30" width="152" height="40" class="dg-box"/><text x="470" y="54.55" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13">Expired</text><path d="M14,80 L384,80" class="dg-line dg-dashed"/><text x="199" y="100" class="dg-note" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11">time to live</text></svg>

glossary.definition: One of several copies of the same cached data, often in different regions.
Shorthand for how close a share is to 100%: six nines is 99.9999%, ten nines is 99.99999999%.
A pattern where the application checks the cache, reads the database on a miss, and then writes the result into the cache.
Reading a database's own log of committed changes so other systems, like a cache, can react to them.

mistakes: Assuming a fill and an invalidation reach the cache in the order they were sent. A delayed fill can land after the invalidation for a newer value and write the old value back.
Keeping the version only inside the cache entry. If the newer entry is evicted, its version goes with it and the cache can no longer tell which value wins.
Treating a stale entry as harmless because it will expire. Without a TTL a missed invalidation can leave it wrong indefinitely, and with a long one it stays wrong until the TTL ends.
comparison:
Both companies keep a cache in front of a database and depend on invalidations to keep it correct, but they spent their effort in different places.

Meta's TAO cache already ran at over a quadrillion queries a day, so the hard problem was finding the rare races that left it wrong, and Meta built Polaris to measure only the inconsistencies a client could see.

Uber was adding a cache to Docstore from scratch, so it fixed the read-versus-invalidation race in the design with row timestamps, made caching opt-in for flows that cannot tolerate staleness, and built a compare mode that reports its own consistency.

why.outcome: After this you can explain what a cache buys you and what it costs.
why.body:
With load balancing, requests spread across many servers, but those servers still read from shared databases, and in read-heavy systems the same data is read again and again. Serving every read from the database means paying for a lot of database capacity.

A cache keeps a copy of hot data in memory, close to the servers, so most reads skip the slow path. The price is that there are now two copies. Every write has to reach the cache too, and until it does, readers can see an old value.

mentalModel.body:
Think of the cache as a notebook next to a filing cabinet. To read, you check the notebook first. If the entry is there, a hit, you use it. If not, a miss, you go to the cabinet, which is the source of truth, and copy the answer into the notebook. That copying is a cache fill.

When the cabinet changes, the notebook is out of date until its entry is crossed out, which is an invalidation, or until it expires after its TTL. The worked example shows a bug that comes from these steps happening in an unexpected order.

a write updates the database, which then invalidates the cached copy.</title><defs><marker id="dg-c-cache-a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M1,1 L9,5 L1,9" class="dg-head"/></marker></defs><rect x="14" y="120" width="110" height="44" class="dg-box"/><text x="69" y="147" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">App</text><rect x="210" y="30" width="140" height="44" class="dg-box dg-accent"/><text x="280" y="57" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">Cache</text><rect x="210" y="210" width="140" height="44" class="dg-box"/><text x="280" y="237" class="dg-label" text-anchor="middle">Database</text><path d="M124,130 C160,100 180,60 206,52" class="dg-line dg-accent" marker-end="url(#dg-c-cache-a)"/><text x="150" y="70" class="dg-note dg-note-accent" text-anchor="middle">1. read</text><text x="400" y="46" class="dg-note dg-note-accent" text-anchor="start">hit: answer now</text><path d="M280,74 L280,206" class="dg-line" marker-end="url(#dg-c-cache-a)"/><text x="288" y="130" class="dg-note" text-anchor="start">2. miss: read the source</text><path d="M262,206 L262,78" class="dg-line dg-dashed" marker-end="url(#dg-c-cache-a)"/><text x="254" y="160" class="dg-note" text-anchor="end">3. fill</text><path d="M124,154 C160,190 180,225 206,232" class="dg-line" marker-end="url(#dg-c-cache-a)"/><text x="150" y="225" class="dg-note" text-anchor="middle">write</text><path d="M350,220 C430,190 430,80 354,58" class="dg-line dg-dashed" marker-end="url(#dg-c-cache-a)"/><text x="440" y="140" class="dg-note" text-anchor="start">invalidate</text><text x="280" y="290" class="dg-note" text-anchor="middle">every copy can be out of date until it is invalidated or expires</text></svg>

steps.explanation: The server asks the cache for the key. A hit returns at once.
On a miss, the server reads the database and writes the value into the cache for the next reader.
Writes go to the source of truth, not to the cache.
The change is sent to the cache to remove or replace the old entry. Uber used the database's own log of committed changes for this.
Every entry has a TTL, so even a missed invalidation cannot leave it wrong forever. A cache with limited room also evicts, meaning drops, entries to make space.
A slow fill can read an old value and write it after the invalidation for a newer one. Storing a version or timestamp with each entry lets the cache keep only the newer value.

workedExample.outcome: After this you can trace a stale-cache race in a real system and see how it was caught and prevented.

steps.explanation: At Meta, a cache fill reads a value from the database.
Before the fill finishes, a write changes the value and an invalidation is sent to the cache.
The invalidation for the new value reaches the cache first; then the delayed fill writes the old value. The cache is now wrong until something evicts the entry.

Meta's Polaris receives the same invalidations, asks every replica for the key, and rechecks flagged samples before reporting (the post's example timescales are one, five and ten minutes), so normal lag (replicas briefly trailing behind a write) is not counted. Over the years, by one measure, TAO went from six to ten nines of writes consistent within five minutes, and Polaris is how Meta measured it.
Uber's Docstore cache prevents the race: Redis keeps a row only if its MySQL timestamp is newer than the one already cached.

Uber also invalidates from the MySQL binary log (the database's record of committed changes) and expires entries after 5 minutes by default, and leaves caching off for flows that need strong consistency.

lesson.checkOutcome: After this you can tell whether you understood the concept before reading the posts.

quiz.question: What is a cache fill?
options: Deleting every entry from the cache so the next reads all have to start from scratch again
Copying the whole database onto disk as a backup that the cache can restore from
Writing a value into the cache after a miss has read it from the database
quiz.why: On a miss the server reads the source of truth and stores the result for the next reader.
wrong: That would be a flush, not a fill.
A fill copies one value into memory, not the whole database.

quiz.question: A fill reads value A. The value changes to B and B's invalidation arrives. Then the fill writes A. The cache keeps no version. What does the cache hold?
options: B, the newer value, because the invalidation arrived before the delayed fill did
Nothing, because the invalidation removed the entry and the late fill was rejected
quiz.why: The delayed fill overwrote the newer state, so the cache holds A until it is evicted or expires.
wrong: The invalidation came first, so the late fill wrote A on top.
The fill wrote A, so the entry exists.

quiz.question: How can a cache refuse a late, older write?
options: Use a bigger cache so older and newer values can sit side by side without clashing
Store a version or timestamp with each entry and keep only the newer one
Read from the cache twice and compare the two answers before trusting either one
quiz.why: Comparing versions lets the cache tell which value is newer, whatever order the writes arrive in.
wrong: Size does not decide which value wins.
Reading twice does not fix what is stored.

quiz.question: Why give entries a TTL even when you invalidate on every write?
options: It makes reads faster because expired entries are skipped without being checked
So a missed invalidation cannot leave an entry wrong forever
Because invalidations are never needed once every entry has an expiry time set
quiz.why: Invalidations can be lost or raced; expiry bounds how long a wrong value can live. Uber, for example, expires entries after 5 minutes by default even when no invalidation arrives.
wrong: Expiry causes extra misses; it does not speed reads.
Invalidation is still the main way changes reach the cache.

quiz.question: Why is a cache used at all, given the staleness risk?
options: Databases cannot store the amount of data that services hold
Caches never go stale because every write also updates the copy straight away
Read-heavy systems would otherwise need far more database capacity
quiz.why: Serving repeated reads from memory is much cheaper than serving them from the database.
wrong: A database can hold all the data. Uber's Docstore stores tens of petabytes. The cost is serving every repeated read from the database.
Caches can go stale. That is the cost being accepted.

quiz.question: Before reporting a stale entry, Meta's checker waits and rechecks. Why?
options: To let normal replication lag settle, so only real inconsistencies are counted
To collect more samples first, because one flagged entry says little about the cache
To let the database finish replicating, since it cannot serve reads during that time
quiz.why: Waiting keeps the metric free of false alarms, so people trust it.
wrong: Each flagged entry is rechecked by itself. The wait is for invalidations that are still on their way, not for gathering a bigger sample.
The database is not what lags here. A cache replica may simply not have processed the invalidation yet, and the wait allows for that.

lesson.postsOutcome: After this you can describe how two companies kept a cache in front of a consistent database correct.
lesson.differOutcome: After this you can explain when to measure inconsistency and when to design it out.
lesson.exercisesOutcome: After this you can apply the concept to a bug, design a cache, and plan for ten times the scale.

exercises.prompt: Users sometimes see an old profile picture for hours after changing it. Invalidation runs on every write. What is likely happening and what do you change?
exercises.answer: A late fill or a lost invalidation left an old value with no expiry. Store a version with each entry and keep only the newer one, and add a TTL as a backstop.
exercises.tradeoffs: Shorter TTLs mean more misses and database load; versions need to be stored and compared on every write. A version kept only in the entry is lost when the entry is evicted.
wrongAnswers: Trusting that invalidations always arrive in order, so changing nothing.
Clearing the whole cache on each write.
Relying on the TTL alone with a very long expiry.

exercises.prompt: Design a cache for a database that many teams share, so each team does not build its own.
exercises.answer: Put the cache in the database's query layer, filled on reads, invalidated from the database's change log, protected by row versions, and opt-in per table or request so strongly consistent flows can skip it. Add a mode that compares cached reads against the database.
exercises.tradeoffs: Cached reads become eventually consistent, so it must be opt-in, and the cache adds one more system to run.
wrongAnswers: Invalidating in the write path, which cannot see which rows a conditional update touched.
Turning caching on for every flow.

exercises.prompt: Traffic grows ten times and you add a second region that must take over during a failover. What do you plan for?
exercises.answer: Keep the other region's cache warm by copying keys, not values, and let it fill from its own database. Shard the cache (split it across machines) differently from the database so one cache failure does not hammer one database shard, and use a circuit breaker (a switch that stops calls to something that keeps failing) to skip failing cache nodes and adaptive timeouts so slow cache calls fall back to the database.
exercises.tradeoffs: Warming costs extra reads in the second region, though only on cache misses. Protection adds moving parts to run.
wrongAnswers: Failing over to a cold cache.
Copying cached values between regions with a second replication system.

next.outcome: After this you can pick the next topic that builds on this one.
next.body: A cache next to your servers helps reads inside your data centre, but users far away still wait on the network. CDNs pick up from there: caching content at the edge, close to users.
